title: One New Language a Year, No Fluency Required
summary: Why learning one new programming or spoken language a year pays off even if you never ship it, how to pick one that stretches you, and how to keep the year small.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
The first evening with a new language is humbling. The editor's open, the docs look friendly, and a ten-line example still takes an hour. A missing import. A type error you've never seen before. A borrow checker that rejects code you were sure was fine. Thirty minutes in, you remember exactly what being a beginner feels like.

That feeling is the point. In The Pragmatic Programmer, Andy Hunt and Dave Thomas suggest learning at least one new language every year as part of investing in your "knowledge portfolio." The matching tip, "Invest Regularly in Your Knowledge Portfolio" (Tip 9), sums it up in one line: "Make learning a habit." Nobody's asking you to get fluent every year. The goal is to stay with an unfamiliar way of thinking long enough to see what it makes easy, what it makes awkward and what it shows you about the tools you already use.

Every language makes different things normal

Alan Perlis said it in one line back in 1982: "A language that doesn't affect the way you think about programming, is not worth knowing" (Epigrams on Programming, no. 19). Syntax is the easy part, the vocabulary. The interesting part is what the language treats as normal.

Two quick examples. In Go, an error is an ordinary return value you check right where it happens, and Rob Pike's post Errors are values shows how to program with errors instead of around them. In Rust, every value has exactly one owner and gets dropped when that owner goes out of scope (The Rust Book, chapter 4). Spend a few weeks with either one and you'll start asking new questions in your day-job code: who handles this error, and who owns this object?

Those questions stay with you even if you never ship a line of Rust. That's the return on the time.

Pick one that stretches a different muscle

Going from Java to Kotlin usually teaches you less than going from Java to Elixir. Peter Norvig's Teach Yourself Programming in Ten Years recommends learning at least half a dozen languages over time and spreading them across styles. Here's his list:

StyleNorvig's examplesWhat it tends to train
Class abstractionsJava, C++Modeling a domain as objects and interfaces
Functional abstractionLisp, ML, HaskellPure functions, immutable data, composing small pieces
Syntactic abstractionLispMacros, code that writes code
Declarative specificationsProlog, C++ templatesSaying what you want and letting the engine work out how
ParallelismClojure, GoDesigning for concurrency from the start

The third column is my own shorthand, not Norvig's. If your daily stack sits in one row, pick next year's language from another.

Keep the year small

A year sounds long, but the work can be tiny. You don't need to build a product in every language. A handful of exercises covers most of what a language has to teach:

  • a small CLI that takes arguments and prints something useful
  • parsing a real file (CSV, JSON, a log) and handling the bad lines
  • calling an HTTP API and dealing with timeouts and errors
  • modeling a tiny domain and writing tests for it
  • reading code from a well-known open-source project in that language

Then write one short note: what felt strange, what you'd like to steal for your main language, what you were happy to leave behind. Skip the note and the year shrinks into a pile of trivia. Write it and you have something to reread when you pick the next language.

Spoken languages count too

Some years the new language might be Japanese or Spanish instead of Zig. The lesson is similar. A sentence that sounds direct in one language can sound rude in another, and some words carry context a translation can't fully move. Even a few months of study makes you more careful with tone.

The Pragmatic Programmer connects the two from the other side: "English is Just Another Programming Language" and "It's Both What You Say and the Way You Say It" are tips 11 and 12 in the book's list. If you write release notes, PR descriptions or error messages for readers in other countries, that extra care shows up in your work right away.

Watch out for the novelty trap

There's a catch. Starting something new every few months feels productive, and it can turn into a way to dodge depth. You never reach the hard middle of anything, so you never get stuck, so you never really learn. The guard is a small, honest scope: one language, one year, one small thing built, one note written. Enough novelty to stretch you, and not so much that it becomes a place to hide.

Norvig's essay is a good counterweight here. The title says it: real expertise takes years of practice. A new language each year sits on top of that depth. It can't stand in for it.

Being a beginner again pays off at work

The best part of a yearly language is the beginner feeling itself. It's uncomfortable, and it's useful. After a month of fighting an unfamiliar compiler, you read a junior teammate's PR differently. You explain things in smaller steps. You remember that expertise is something you keep earning through practice, and every new language shows you how far away the next level still is.

Try this year

  • Look at the table and pick a language from a row your daily stack doesn't touch.
  • Block one evening a week for a month. Do the CLI and the file-parsing exercises first.
  • Keep a running list of what feels strange. That list is where the learning is.
  • At the end, write down one habit you'll bring back to your main language.
